transcript.message: I would like to know a little bit more about how this has been kind of affecting your your personal life and your social life for example uh your life at home with your. Roommates or maybe other friendships, relationships with your family. Has it gotten in the way of that?
Yeah, I've definitely pulled away from people—I don't go out as much, and I feel kind of isolated from my friends and roommates.

Yeah, that's a very difficult feeling. And you mentioned that this has also been going on for a year. To this kind of year long history of you feeling this sense of worry. Has it occurred previously in your life or is this the first time that this has happened?
This is the first time it's been this bad or lasted this long. Before, I had stress, but nothing like this.
Hm okay okay. Got it um uh, I would like to ask you a few more questions about how you're doing right now um. And kind of less related to your previous symptoms. Would that be okay?
Yeah, that's fine, go ahead and ask.
Could you describe your mood for me um lately like what, how have your spirits been?
Honestly, I've just felt pretty on edge and worried most of the time, not really relaxed or happy lately.
Would you say you've been troubled by sadness?
Not really sad, just more anxious and restless than anything else.
Okay yeah yeah, I understand um and aside from this kind of general worry that you've been experiencing. Do you ever experience periods of feeling panicked?
No, I don't really get panic attacks—it's more just this constant anxiety, not big rushes of panic.

And then another question that I have to ask, which is a little sensitive, but it's really important we ask it to everyone. Have any thoughts of harming yourself? For others or ending your own life crossed your mind.
No, I haven't had any thoughts like that.
Okay, got it. And has, so you mentioned that you've been having trouble with your sleep. I'm wondering if your appetite has. Changed at all.
My appetite is about the same—it's just the sleep that's really thrown off.
Oh sorry continue please.
Yeah, I just usually have trouble falling asleep, then I wake up feeling tired all day.
Um, and do you have any history of sleep problems that you know of like has anyone ever told you that you have sleep apnea or anything like that?
No, nobody's ever said anything like that to me before, and I haven't had sleep issues until this anxiety started.
And how has your energy levels and your concentration been since you've, you know, been more worried and getting less sleep?
My energy has definitely dropped, and it's way harder to focus at work or when I'm doing things around the house.
Okay, got it um i'd like to ask you some more questions that are specifically related to anxiety symptoms. Is that all right with you?
Yeah, that's fine, go ahead and ask whatever you need to.
Great um have you ever experienced repetitive, unwanted thoughts or felt the need to repeat certain behaviors unnecessarily?
No, I haven't really had those kinds of thoughts or felt like I had to do things over and over.
Okay um do you have any specific fears which you consider irrational?
No, not really—it's more just general worry about everything instead of one specific fear.
And are you troubled by an inability to relax, would you say that goes along with the worry you describe?
Definitely, I find it almost impossible to just unwind or feel calm these days.
Understanding and do you have any history that you're aware of of trauma? So like for example, physical or sexual abuse?
No, I don't have any history like that.
Got it. Thank you for answering those questions. I know sometimes they can be sensitive and a little difficult for sure.
Yeah, I get it. Thanks for being understanding about it.

Yeah, of course. And kind of while we're on the topic of mental health, I know you mentioned that you hadn't experienced, you know, persistent worry like this. Before the past year. Do you have any other history of any emotional or psychiatric illnesses that you're aware of or any substance? Issues.
No, nothing like that. I don't have any history of other mental health issues or substance problems.
Got it.
Alright, let me know if you need anything else from me.
I think that sums it up mostly. Is there anything else that you wanted to share about what you've been experiencing or any questions that you have?
Yeah, I guess I just want to know—how do you know for sure this is just anxiety and not something physical?

Well, we certainly can rule out certain things that can contribute to symptoms that are, that can manifest like anxiety that are. Different from you know just a psychiatric like illness of a generalized anxiety for example um so we can certainly. Run some tests for common things that would rule it out but I would say that the the duration that you've been experiencing your symptoms. As well as the way you characterize them does sound quite like a generalized anxiety picture that we commonly see.
Okay, I get that, but what kind of tests do people usually do to check for other causes?

Well, for example, you mentioned the the sleep disturbances so so we could do a sleep study. It does sound though more like you're having. That's keeping you up at night rather than problems with getting actual restful sleep. But we could do a sleep study, for example. We could also do some blood work to look for, you know, rule out things that could be causing lower energy like we could make. Make sure that you're not anemic or hypothyroid, for example.
That makes sense. If the blood work and all that come back normal, I guess that would make it clearer this is anxiety, right?

Yeah, and the other way that we diagnose it is we use, you know, diagnostic criteria to help us, help us paint a picture. So whenever. We're you know seeing someone for for an issue that's potentially psychological or psychiatric in nature we really look at everything there. Experiencing a very holistic picture and we kind of compare that against all of our criteria to kind of ascertain what is the. Likely diagnosis and if it's not that, what else could it be? But what you are describing sounds quite a lot like generalized anxiety. With the constant worry about minor and large life events, which is now starting to interfere with your with your day to day and your social life as well.
Okay, got it. I just appreciate hearing a real explanation, so thank you—helps me feel a little more confident in what's going on.
Yeah, i'm glad to hear that um did you have any other questions for me before I leave the room and go speak with my preceptor who's overseeing me today?
No, I think you've answered my main questions. I'll wait to hear what the next steps are from you and your team.
Okay great we'll be back shortly. All right.
Sounds good, thanks for letting me know.

1.textFeedbackReport:
{
  "feedback": "Introduction and Rapport Building: While you proceeded directly into asking about the impact on her personal and social life, consider beginning the session with a warm greeting and a brief introduction of yourself and the session’s purpose. This helps set a welcoming tone and build immediate rapport. 

Assessment and Understanding: You did a good job exploring various aspects of Alexandra’s experience by addressing social implications, mood, sleep, appetite, and concentration. Your questioning allowed her to divulge important details about the chronicity and impact of her symptoms. In future sessions, you might also gently inquire about her coping methods or past strategies to understand how she has managed stress previously. 

Communication Skills: Your style of questioning was clear and empathetic. You acknowledged her struggles (e.g., “that’s a very difficult feeling”) and listened carefully to her responses. To further enhance communication, consider reflective statements to validate her feelings and to ensure that you have fully captured her emotional experience. 

Confidentiality and Ethical Considerations: While the session was handled discreetly, it would be beneficial to explicitly mention that the information shared is confidential and explain the boundaries of that confidentiality at the outset. This explicit reassurance can increase the patient’s comfort level, especially when sensitive topics are discussed. 

Session Closing: The session was brought to a close by checking if she had any further questions, which is positive, but a more structured closure would be helpful. Providing a brief summary of the discussion, outlining next steps, and mentioning follow-up plans or practice assignments (if any) would leave the patient with clear expectations and a sense of direction for recovery. 

Application of Psychiatric Diagnosis: Your approach in discussing testing and explaining the differential diagnostic process was thoughtful. You integrated information from her history and symptoms to support a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder using established criteria. For future interactions, continue to ask probing questions that assess the full spectrum of symptoms, including ruling out other conditions, so as to secure a confident and accurate diagnosis.",
  "extendedQuestions": [
    "How might you modify your opening statements in future sessions to create a stronger initial rapport with patients?",
    "Can you think of specific reflective statements or clarifications you might use to ensure patients feel fully understood when discussing sensitive topics?",
    "What strategies could you implement to explicitly address confidentiality at the start of your sessions?",
    "In terms of closure, what key components would you include to ensure the patient leaves with a clear understanding of the next steps?"
  ]
}
